definition: A geospatial foundation model (GFM), also referred to as an Earth observation foundation model, represents a paradigm shift in Earth system modeling by utilizing data-centric artificial intelligence (DCAI) to train on petabytes of structured and unstructured geoscientific data.
details: Unlike conventional, task-specific deep learning systems, GFMs use massive cross-disciplinary datasets to model the Earth's interactive and complex dynamics, offering highly flexible task specifications, multimodal inputs/outputs, and advanced geoscientific knowledge representation.

explainer.lead: A geospatial foundation model is a general-purpose AI model for learning from vast and varied information about Earth. It matters because one model can support many Earth-observation tasks and data types instead of requiring a separate task-specific system each time.

tiers.eli5: Imagine learning from a huge library about land, water, weather, and maps instead of practicing just one puzzle. A geospatial foundation model learns from enormous amounts of information about Earth, so people can ask it to help with different Earth-observation jobs. It can work with several kinds of information and produce different kinds of answers.
tiers.practitioner: Use a GFM as a shared pretrained basis for Earth-observation work rather than training a separate task-specific network for every job. The setting is large-scale, data-centric training over structured and unstructured, cross-disciplinary geoscientific data, with multimodal inputs and outputs and flexible task specifications. The main pitfalls are the data scale and assuming that flexibility alone guarantees reliable transfer to a new task.
tiers.paperLevel: A GFM is a data-centric AI model trained on petabyte-scale structured and unstructured geoscientific data to represent interacting Earth-system dynamics. Its intended distinction from task-specific deep learning is flexible task specification, multimodal input/output, and cross-disciplinary geoscientific knowledge representation. These properties define the paradigm; they do not by themselves establish accuracy or generalization for a particular task.

explainer.example: A team could train a GFM on satellite observations together with other structured and unstructured geoscientific records. It could then ask the same model to help map flooded areas from suitable Earth-observation inputs, rather than building a separate task-specific deep-learning system from scratch.

usedIn.name: Earth observation

usedIn.name: Earth system modeling
usedIn.detail: Represents interactive and complex dynamics learned from cross-disciplinary data.

usedIn.name: Geoscientific analysis
usedIn.detail: Uses shared knowledge representations across structured and unstructured geoscientific information.

explainer.intuition: Instead of teaching a model one narrow job, train it broadly on many kinds of information about Earth. The resulting shared model can then be directed toward different tasks and work with multiple input and output forms.
howItWorks: Gather petabytes of structured and unstructured geoscientific data across disciplines.
Use data-centric AI to train a shared model of Earth's complex, interacting dynamics.
Specify the desired task flexibly and provide inputs in supported modalities.
Produce task-relevant outputs while reusing the model's geoscientific knowledge representation.
explainer.whyItMatters: GFMs aim to make Earth system modeling more reusable and adaptable across tasks, disciplines, and data modalities. Their data-centric approach is intended to capture interactions that narrowly trained, task-specific systems may not represent.
misconceptions: A GFM is not simply a conventional task-specific model with more layers; its cross-disciplinary training and flexible use are central.
Flexible task specification does not mean every Earth-science question is solved automatically.
Multimodal input and output do not by themselves guarantee accurate results on a new task.
